chunks.heading: Architecture
chunks.text: --- title: "Architecture" description: "How PocketMageOS is put together: the boot path, the dispatch state machine, the two-display model, storage, and the two ways apps run." --- PocketMageOS is a single-core-visible cooperative state machine on an ESP32-S3. One variable, `CurrentAppState`, decides which app owns the keyboard and the screens; the main loop routes every keystroke and every screen refresh to that app's handlers. This page is the map of the whole system and where each part is documented in depth.

On power-up the OS mounts the SD card, initializes the displays and keyboard, and loads persistent settings from NVS. It then decides which app to enter based on how the device woke: - Normal boot enters HOME, unless `HOME_ON_BOOT` is off. - A wake with a held shortcut key enters the mapped app (for example `n` opens TXT). The mapping is `bootShortcutApp()` in `UTILS.cpp`. - A wake from now-later returns to the app that was active before sleep, with its saved state restored.

Two functions switch on `CurrentAppState`: - `processKB()` routes each keypress to the active app's keyboard handler. - `applicationEinkHandler()` routes each screen refresh to the active app's draw handler. The device pairs a slow, sharp 320x240 E-Ink panel with a fast 256x32 OLED. Anything that benefits from instant feedback - prompts, status, timers - goes to the OLED; anything that benefits from a large readable page - notes, files, calendars - goes to the E-Ink. The E-Ink panel is guarded by a recursive mutex and refreshed from a background task, so code in other tasks must respect that boundary. The display APIs are in the [PocketMage Library reference](../reference/pocketmage-library.md), with the full per-module contract on the [SDK API docs](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/api/).

The OS keeps shared runtime state in `globals.h`: the active app, the home sub-state, the re-init flag, persistent preferences, the active filesystem handle, and the idle-timeout lockout. Files live on a microSD card, reached through the library's SD module (`PM_SD()`). chunks.heading: How apps run
chunks.text: The OS tracks a working file and an editing file for save/load flows, and installed ELF apps live in four slots under `/apps/slot1` through `/apps/slot4`, tracked in NVS as `ELFINFO1` through `ELFINFO4`. Native and ELF apps share the three-function shape; they differ only in where the code ships and how it is loaded. - **Native apps** are compiled into the firmware under `src/OS_APPS/` and wired into the dispatch switch. See [Native Apps](../guides/native-apps.md). - **ELF apps** are built separately against the SDK, packed with an overlay sidecar, and loaded from the SD card at runtime by `src/elf_runner.cpp`. The runner relocates the base image with `esp_elf`, pages the app's code into executable RAM through the `elf_overlay` runtime, and runs the entry in its own 16 KB task while the OS loop and the E-Ink task stand down. Returning from the entry unloads the app and reopens HOME. See [ELF Apps](../guides/elf-apps.md), and the SDK's [App ABI](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/app-abi/) and [Overlay format](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/overlay/). ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant OS as OS loop participant RN as elf_runner participant EE as esp_elf participant OV as elf_overlay participant APP as app task OS->>RN: launch installed ELF (slot) RN->>EE: relocate base image from SD RN->>OV: load overlay sidecar, apply redirects RN->>APP: start 16 KB task, run entry Note over OS,APP: OS loop and E-Ink task stand down APP-->>RN: entry returns RN->>OV: unload overlay RN->>OS: reopen HOME ```

chunks.heading: Build Environments & PlatformIO Setup
chunks.text: --- title: "Build Environments & PlatformIO Setup" description: "How to set up PlatformIO and build PocketMage firmware on Linux, macOS, and Windows." --- PocketMage firmware is built with [PlatformIO](https://platformio.org/). The build configuration lives in `Code/PocketMageOS/platformio.ini` and defines two environments that produce the firmware variants. Third-party apps are not built in this tree; they are compiled against the PocketMage SDK (see [ELF Apps](../guides/elf-apps.md)).

chunks.heading: PocketMageOS
chunks.text: --- title: "PocketMageOS" description: "The PocketMage operating system and app runtime." --- PocketMageOS is the operating system layer of the firmware. It boots the device, starts and switches apps, routes keyboard input, dispatches screen updates, and tracks the system state that every app depends on. This page explains how that runtime works and where the code lives. ::: grids ::: grid ::: card "Boot and route" icon:play Starts the right app, routes keyboard input, and keeps screen updates on the right handler. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Manage state" icon:settings Tracks timeout, sleep, lock, and the active app. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Bridge hardware" icon:cpu Coordinates the shared hardware layer, storage, and device helpers. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Support apps" icon:box Native apps and ELF apps plug into the same runtime model. ::: ::: :::

chunks.heading: The app runtime model
chunks.text: Coordinates the shared hardware layer, storage, and device helpers. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Support apps" icon:box Native apps and ELF apps plug into the same runtime model. ::: ::: ::: Every PocketMage app is a set of three functions. The OS calls them at the right time; the app never drives the loop itself. 1. **`*_INIT()`** - runs once when the app is entered. Sets app state and prepares the screen. 2. **`processKB_*()`** - runs on every keypress. The app reads the key, updates its state, and queues a redraw. 3. **`einkHandler_*()`** - runs when the screen needs updating. The app draws the current state to the E-Ink buffer. The dispatch loop in `PocketMageV3.cpp` owns the switch between these handlers. It is a `switch (CurrentAppState)` that routes each keystroke and each E-Ink refresh to the active app. Adding an app means adding a case to that switch and an entry to the `AppState` enum in `globals.h`. The spots are marked `// ADD APP CASES HERE`.

chunks.heading: How boot works
chunks.text: to the active app. Adding an app means adding a case to that switch and an entry to the `AppState` enum in `globals.h`. The spots are marked `// ADD APP CASES HERE`. On power-up, PocketMageOS mounts the SD card, initializes the displays and keyboard, and loads persistent settings from NVS. It then checks which app to enter. This depends on how the device was woken: - **Normal boot** - enters the home app (unless the `HOME_ON_BOOT` setting is off). - **Woken from sleep with a shortcut key** - enters the app mapped to that key. For example, pressing `N` while sleeping opens TXT. The mapping is `bootShortcutApp()` in `UTILS.cpp`. - **Woken from now-later** - returns to the app that was active before sleep, restoring its saved state.

chunks.heading: State the OS tracks
chunks.text: For example, pressing `N` while sleeping opens TXT. The mapping is `bootShortcutApp()` in `UTILS.cpp`. - **Woken from now-later** - returns to the app that was active before sleep, restoring its saved state. The OS keeps shared runtime state in `globals.h`. The pieces you will meet most often: - `CurrentAppState` - which app is active. This drives the dispatch switch. - `CurrentHOMEState` - the home screen mode (`HOME_HOME` or `NOWLATER`). - `newState` - a flag that tells the loop to re-run `*_INIT()` for the target app. - `disableTimeout` - a global lockout so an app can prevent idle sleep while it is busy. - `prefs` - persistent preferences stored in NVS. - `global_fs` - the active filesystem handle. The timeout system is also part of the OS. After `IDLE_TIME` without input, the OS shows the mage idle state; after `TIMEOUT` seconds it sleeps. Apps can reset the idle clock with `resetIdle()` or block it entirely with `disableTimeout`.

chunks.heading: How apps reach the hardware
chunks.text: the OS. After `IDLE_TIME` without input, the OS shows the mage idle state; after `TIMEOUT` seconds it sleeps. Apps can reset the idle clock with `resetIdle()` or block it entirely with `disableTimeout`. Apps do not talk to hardware directly. They call the PocketMage Library, which owns the physical devices. `OLED().sysMessage(...)` flashes a message, `EINK().refresh()` pushes the E-Ink buffer, `KB()` handles key state, and `SD()` handles storage. The library is the only layer that knows the pins. This is what lets the same app code build for native, ELF, and future hardware revisions. See [PocketMage Library](../reference/pocketmage-library.md) for the full module map.

chunks.heading: Native vs ELF apps
chunks.text: is the only layer that knows the pins. This is what lets the same app code build for native, ELF, and future hardware revisions. See [PocketMage Library](../reference/pocketmage-library.md) for the full module map. - **Native apps** live in `src/OS_APPS/`, are compiled into the firmware, and are wired into the dispatch switch. - **ELF apps** are compiled separately against the PocketMage SDK into a `.app.elf`, packed with an overlay sidecar, and loaded from the SD card at runtime through the app loader. No firmware reflash is involved. The runner (`src/elf_runner.cpp`) relocates the base image with `esp_elf`, then pages the app's code into executable RAM through the `elf_overlay` runtime, and runs the app's entry in its own task while the OS loop stands down. Both follow the same three-function shape. The difference is where the code ships and how it is loaded. See [ELF Apps](../guides/elf-apps.md) for the device side, [Making Apps](../guides/making-apps.md) for the workflow, and the [SDK docs](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/) for the binary contract.

chunks.heading: What is PocketMage?
chunks.text: --- title: "What is PocketMage?" description: "A short explanation of the PocketMage device and firmware stack." --- PocketMage is a clamshell PDA built around an ESP32-S3. It is open-source hardware and software, designed to be built at home, hacked, and extended. This page explains the device and the two software layers that run on it. ::: grids ::: grid ::: card "Dual displays" icon:monitor A 320x240 E-Ink panel for the main workspace and a 256x32 OLED for status and fast feedback. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Full keyboard" icon:keyboard A tactile thumb keyboard with four layers: normal, shift, function, and function plus shift. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Two software layers" icon:layers PocketMageOS handles apps and state; the PocketMage Library handles the hardware. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Open and extendable" icon:wrench Build apps with C++ or run Wrench scripts from the terminal. Load third-party apps at runtime. ::: ::: :::

chunks.heading: The hardware
chunks.text: handles the hardware. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Open and extendable" icon:wrench Build apps with C++ or run Wrench scripts from the terminal. Load third-party apps at runtime. ::: ::: ::: The main display is a 3.1" 1-bit E-Ink panel (320x240). E-Ink is sharp and power efficient, but slow to update, so a small OLED sits below it for status text, prompts, and feedback that needs to appear instantly. The keyboard is a matrix driven by a TCA8418 IC, which is why it can support four separate key layers. The device runs on an ESP32-S3 with 16 MB flash and WiFi and Bluetooth radios. Storage lives on a microSD card. Everything else - RTC, buzzer, battery management, USB, and an expansion port with I2C/SPI/UART breakouts - is exposed to software through the shared library.

chunks.heading: The two software layers
chunks.text: Bluetooth radios. Storage lives on a microSD card. Everything else - RTC, buzzer, battery management, USB, and an expansion port with I2C/SPI/UART breakouts - is exposed to software through the shared library. PocketMage firmware is split into two layers so that apps stay small. - **PocketMageOS** is the operating system. It owns boot, app switching, state, keyboard routing, and the screen dispatch loop. If you are changing how the device behaves, you are working in PocketMageOS. - **PocketMage Library** is the reusable hardware and UI support layer, shipped as the PocketMage SDK and vendored at `Code/PocketMageOS/lib/PocketMage_SDK/`. It wraps the display, storage, keyboard, audio, clock, and system helpers so apps never talk to hardware directly. The split matters because both native apps and third-party ELF apps build on the same library. An app does three jobs - initialize, handle input, draw - and uses the library for everything else. Native apps are compiled into the firmware; ELF apps are built separately against the SDK and loaded from the SD card at runtime. The SDK is documented on its own [SDK documentation site](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/).

chunks.heading: ELF Apps
chunks.text: --- title: "ELF Apps" description: "How third-party PocketMage apps are built, installed, and loaded by the OS at runtime." --- Third-party apps are compiled outside the OS into a `.app.elf`, packed into a `.tar` with an overlay sidecar and an icon, and installed at runtime through the app loader. No firmware reflash is involved. This page covers the app from the OS side: how the loader runs it, where installed apps live, and what an app can rely on. The binary contract itself, the build tooling, and the full symbol surface are owned by the SDK documentation and are not duplicated here. For building and shipping an app, start with the SDK docs: - [App ABI](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/app-abi/) - the binary contract - [Overlay format](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/overlay/) - the `.elfo` sidecar - [Building apps](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/build/) - the toolchain and `make` targets - [Symbols](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/symbols/) - the host export surface

chunks.heading: What an ELF app is
chunks.text: SDK docs: - [App ABI](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/app-abi/) - the binary contract - [Overlay format](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/overlay/) - the `.elfo` sidecar - [Building apps](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/build/) - the toolchain and `make` targets - [Symbols](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/symbols/) - the host export surface An ELF app is a standalone 32-bit `ET_DYN` program linked against the PocketMage SDK with `PM_TARGET_APP`. It links `-nostdlib`, so it ships no runtime of its own; everything it references, from `malloc` to the `pm_*` API, resolves from the host at load time. The runner (`src/elf_runner.cpp`) loads an installed app in two stages. It reads the `.app.elf` from the SD card and relocates the base image with `esp_elf`, then loads the matching `.elfo` overlay sidecar, which pages the app's code into executable RAM on demand and patches ISA-specific relocations. The entry (`app_main`) then runs in its own 16 KB task on core 1. While the app runs, the OS loop and the E-Ink task stand down and the app owns the UI through the host singletons. Exiting is a `return` from `app_main`. No reboot is needed: the runner unloads the overlay, deinitializes the base image, and reopens HOME.

chunks.heading: Packaging and installing
chunks.text: and the app owns the UI through the host singletons. Exiting is a `return` from `app_main`. No reboot is needed: the runner unloads the overlay, deinitializes the base image, and reopens HOME. 1. Build the app into `<name>.app.elf` and its `<name>.elfo` overlay sidecar. 2. Pack them with a 40x40 `<name>_ICON.bin` and an optional `app.properties` manifest into a plain `.tar` (`make pack` does this). 3. Copy the `.tar` onto the SD card, typically over USB. 4. Open the app loader on the device and use the swap action to install it into one of the four slots. Installed apps live in `/apps/slot1` through `/apps/slot4` on the SD card and are tracked in NVS under `ELFINFO1` through `ELFINFO4`. Launch an installed app from the home screen by typing `A`, `B`, `C`, or `D`, or from the loader.

chunks.heading: The manifest (`app.properties`)
chunks.text: on the SD card and are tracked in NVS under `ELFINFO1` through `ELFINFO4`. Launch an installed app from the home screen by typing `A`, `B`, `C`, or `D`, or from the loader. The loader reads an optional `app.properties` from the app's slot directory (up to 1024 bytes). Recognized fields are `name`, `version`, `author`, and `scope`. The first three become the app's display metadata and are passed to `app_main` as `argv`. `scope` (default `all`) restricts which `pm_*` symbols the app may resolve: anything outside its scope fails to resolve, so a mis-scoped app is rejected at load rather than reaching an API it did not declare. The runtime baseline (libc, libstdc++, ESP-IDF) stays available at any scope.

chunks.text: scope fails to resolve, so a mis-scoped app is rejected at load rather than reaching an API it did not declare. Do not call functions from `src/OS_APPS/`. - Keep the app self-contained and link against the SDK only. - Use the PocketMage library for hardware access, exactly like native apps. - The host exports a curated symbol set (generated into `src/ELF_SYMS/esp_all_symbol.cpp`), including `pocketmage_sdk_version` for version checks. A symbol outside that set must be added to the SDK surface before an app can resolve it.

chunks.text: --- title: "Making Apps" description: "How to create PocketMage apps: native apps in the OS and ELF apps sideloaded at runtime." --- PocketMage apps come in two forms: native apps that ship inside PocketMageOS, and ELF apps that are sideloaded onto the device later. Native apps are the focus of this page; the full path for sideloaded apps is the [ELF Apps](elf-apps.md) guide. ::: grids ::: grid ::: card "Native apps" icon:terminal Compiled into the OS and wired into the app dispatch switch. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "ELF apps" icon:package Compiled standalone, loaded from the SD card at runtime. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Native shape" icon:code Native apps are three functions: init, handle input, draw. ::: ::: :::

chunks.heading: The basic app shape
chunks.text: apps" icon:package Compiled standalone, loaded from the SD card at runtime. ::: ::: ::: grid ::: card "Native shape" icon:code Native apps are three functions: init, handle input, draw. ::: ::: ::: Every PocketMage app has the same three jobs, and they map directly to three functions. 1. **Initialize state** - run once when the app opens. Set up whatever the app needs and mark the screen for a redraw. 2. **Process keyboard input** - run on every keypress. Read the key, update app state, and queue a redraw. 3. **Draw the screen** - run when the E-Ink needs to update. Render the current app state. This pattern is visible in `Code/PocketMageOS/include/globals.h` (the prototypes) and in the app files under `Code/PocketMageOS/src/OS_APPS/`.

chunks.heading: Start with the template
chunks.text: 3. **Draw the screen** - run when the E-Ink needs to update. Render the current app state. This pattern is visible in `Code/PocketMageOS/include/globals.h` (the prototypes) and in the app files under `Code/PocketMageOS/src/OS_APPS/`. The app template is your starting point: - [APP_TEMPLATE.cpp](https://github.com/TalismanDesign/PocketMage_PDA/blob/main/Code/PocketMageOS/src/APP_TEMPLATE.cpp) It defines the three entry points a compiled-in app needs: ```cpp #include <globals.h> #if PM_TARGET_APP void APP_INIT() { // 1. set up app state } void processKB_APP() { // 2. handle a keypress } void einkHandler_APP() { // 3. draw the screen } #endif ```

chunks.heading: Building the app step by step
chunks.text: #if PM_TARGET_APP void APP_INIT() { // 1. set up app state } void processKB_APP() { // 2. handle a keypress } void einkHandler_APP() { // 3. draw the screen } #endif ``` 1. **Decide native vs ELF.** If the app belongs to the device experience, make it native. If it is third-party or experimental, make it an ELF app so it can be installed and removed without reflashing the OS. 2. **Pick the shared helpers.** Browse the [PocketMage Library](../reference/pocketmage-library.md) before writing anything. Prompts (`textPrompt()`), file selection (`fileWizardMini()`), and timeouts (`checkTimeout()`) already exist; do not reimplement them. 3. **Wire it into the OS (native only).** Add an `AppState` entry, the three prototypes, and the `switch` cases marked `// ADD APP CASES HERE` in `PocketMageV3.cpp`. Then add a home-screen command if you want it launchable by name. 4. **Test the keyboard path first.** Get a keypress into your handler and onto the OLED before worrying about the E-Ink. 5. **Test the E-Ink path second.** Make sure drawing and refresh behave, including fast partial refreshes. 6. **Check timeout, wake, and save last.** Confirm the app resets the idle clock, handles sleep/wake without corrupting state, and saves before exit where it should.

chunks.heading: Native Apps
chunks.text: --- title: "Native Apps" description: "How PocketMageOS native apps are structured." --- Native apps live inside PocketMageOS and are compiled into the firmware. Each one is a set of three functions wired into the OS dispatch loop. This page explains the pattern and the exact wiring you need when adding one.

chunks.heading: The pattern
chunks.text: compiled into the firmware. Each one is a set of three functions wired into the OS dispatch loop. This page explains the pattern and the exact wiring you need when adding one. Every native app follows this shape: - `*_INIT()` - set up app state and enter the app - `processKB_*()` - handle keyboard input - `einkHandler_*()` - draw the screen The names are per-app, not generic. Examples from the codebase: | App | Init | Keyboard | Draw | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Home | `HOME_INIT()` | `processKB_HOME()` | `einkHandler_HOME()` | | TXT | `TXT_INIT()` | `processKB_TXT_NEW()` | `einkHandler_TXT_NEW()` | | FileWiz | `FILEWIZ_INIT()` | `processKB_FILEWIZ()` | `einkHandler_FILEWIZ()` | | Calendar | `CALENDAR_INIT()` | `processKB_CALENDAR()` | `einkHandler_CALENDAR()` | | Tasks | `TASKS_INIT()` | `processKB_TASKS()` | `einkHandler_TASKS()` | | Journal | `JOURNAL_INIT()` | `processKB_JOURNAL()` | `einkHandler_JOURNAL()` | | Settings | `SETTINGS_INIT()` | `processKB_SETTINGS()` | `einkHandler_SETTINGS()` | | Loader | `APPLOADER_INIT()` | `processKB_APPLOADER()` | `einkHandler_APPLOADER()` | | Terminal | `TERMINAL_INIT()` | `processKB_TERMINAL()` | `einkHandler_TERMINAL()` |

chunks.text: --- title: "PocketMage Library" description: "Shared hardware, UI, and system modules used by PocketMage." --- The PocketMage Library is the shared hardware, UI, and system layer the firmware links in-process. chunks.heading: Scripting Example: Basic Input/Output
chunks.text: --- title: "Scripting Example: Basic Input/Output" description: "A simple PocketMage script demonstrating user input, OLED output, and terminal printing." --- ```c // PocketMage scripting example // Based on Wrench by jingoro2112 (GH) // Edit with potion: pot example.c // Compile and run: brew example.c // Declare a variable var x = ""; // "" indicates str // Prompt user to enter number // Set x to entered number x = prompt("Enter a number"); // Display x on OLED oledWord(x); // Print x to terminal print(x); // Update the terminal // (refresh the OLED) updateTerm(); // Initialize an iteration var i var i = 0; // Loop while i < x // Use toInt to convert str to int while (i < toInt(x)) { // Iterate i = i + 1; // Display i on OLED oledWord(i); // Wait 500ms delay(500); } // Print the final i to the term print(i); // Generate a random number var randomInt = random(0, 100); print("Random Number: " + randomInt); // Update the terminal // (refresh the OLED) updateTerm(); ```

chunks.heading: Scripting
chunks.text: --- title: "Scripting" description: "Scripting reference and examples for the PocketMage TERMINAL app (Wrench)." --- The PocketMage TERMINAL app runs scripts written in Wrench, a lightweight C-like scripting language. Scripts can draw to the E-Ink and OLED displays, handle input, and talk to the rest of the system through the PocketMage library surface. Wrench is a small interpreted language with a familiar `if` / `while` / `var` syntax. On PocketMage it is embedded inside the TERMINAL app, so every script is a `.c` file on the SD card that the terminal compiles and runs on demand.

chunks.heading: What Wrench is for
chunks.text: `while` / `var` syntax. On PocketMage it is embedded inside the TERMINAL app, so every script is a `.c` file on the SD card that the terminal compiles and runs on demand. Wrench sits one level above a native app. It trades raw performance for convenience: - **Automation** - script repeated terminal workflows instead of typing them each time - **Custom screens** - draw to the E-Ink or OLED with a few function calls - **Prototyping** - test an idea in a script before writing it as a native app - **Device control** - read the clock, battery, keyboard, and touch sensors from a script Because scripts run in the TERMINAL app, they already have access to everything the terminal can reach: the displays, the SD card, prompts, and the shared system helpers.

chunks.heading: Script lifecycle
chunks.text: sensors from a script Because scripts run in the TERMINAL app, they already have access to everything the terminal can reach: the displays, the SD card, prompts, and the shared system helpers. 1. **Edit** - create or open a `.c` script in TXT, or use the terminal's editor. Save it to the SD card. 2. **Compile** - run `brew <script>.c` in the TERMINAL app to compile and execute it. 3. **Run** - the terminal interprets the script. `print()` sends output to the terminal buffer, `updateTerm()` paints it to the OLED. The example scripts at the top of the page double as runnable tests: [Basic Input/Output](example-c.md) walks through the whole edit-to-run flow.

chunks.text: --- title: "Scripting Example: E-Ink Drawing" description: "A PocketMage script demonstrating drawing shapes and text on the E-Ink display." --- The E-Ink display is 320x240 pixels. Coordinates use the top-left origin. ```c // PocketMage E-Ink scripting example // Based on Wrench by jingoro2112 (GH) // Edit with potion: pot ink.c // Compile and run: brew ink.c // Colors/clr: 1 - Black, 0 - White delay(1000); // Draw shapes on a white background inkBackground(0); // background color inkRect(10, 20, 50, 25, 1, 0); // x,y,w,h,line clr,fill clr inkCircle(100, 50, 30, 1, 1); // x,y,r,line clr,fill clr inkText(10, 100, 2, 1, "PocketMage!"); // x,y,size,color,text updateInk(); // update E-Ink display delay(3000); // Draw shapes on a black background inkBackground(1); // background color inkRect(20, 10, 25, 50, 0, 1); // x,y,w,h,line clr,fill clr inkCircle(120, 60, 35, 0, 0); // x,y,r,line clr,fill clr inkText(30, 120, 3, 0, "Hello World!"); // x,y,size,color,text updateInk(); // update E-Ink display delay(3000); ```

chunks.text: --- title: "Scripting Example: OLED Drawing" description: "A PocketMage script demonstrating drawing shapes and text on the OLED display." --- The OLED is 256x32 pixels. Coordinates use the top-left origin, so the horizontal center is x = 128. ```c // PocketMage OLED scripting example // Based on Wrench by jingoro2112 (GH) // Edit with potion: pot oled-c.c // Compile and run: brew oled-c.c // Colors/clr: 1 - Black, 0 - White delay(1000); // Draw shapes on a white background oledBackground(0); // background color oledRect(10, 10, 25, 5, 1, 0); // x,y,w,h,line clr,fill clr oledCircle(128, 10, 8, 1); // x,y,r,line clr oledText(10, 20, 2, 1, "PocketMage!"); // x,y,size,color,text updateOled(); // update OLED display delay(3000); // Draw shapes on a black background oledBackground(1); // background color oledRect(10, 10, 25, 5, 0, 1); // x,y,w,h,line clr,fill clr oledCircle(128, 10, 8, 0); // x,y,r,line clr oledText(10, 20, 2, 0, "Hello World!"); // x,y,size,color,text updateOled(); // update OLED display delay(3000); ```

chunks.heading: What it shows
chunks.text: oledRect(10, 10, 25, 5, 0, 1); // x,y,w,h,line clr,fill clr oledCircle(128, 10, 8, 0); // x,y,r,line clr oledText(10, 20, 2, 0, "Hello World!"); // x,y,size,color,text updateOled(); // update OLED display delay(3000); ``` - `oledBackground()` fills the OLED buffer. - `oledRect()` and `oledCircle()` draw into the buffer. - `oledText()` renders text at a font size. - `updateOled()` pushes the buffer to the screen and clears it.

chunks.heading: PocketMage SD Card Formatting Guide
chunks.text: --- title: "Format a MicroSD Card for PocketMage" description: "Guide to formatting SD cards for compatibility with PocketMage." --- ::: callout danger "These steps erase the card" Everything on the card is destroyed. Back up your data before you start, and double-check the disk identifier at every step so you do not wipe the wrong device. ::: This guide formats an SD card so PocketMage can mount it. The device reads a single FAT32 primary partition on an MBR partition table with 32 KB clusters; anything else is not detected reliably.

chunks.heading: Supported SD card requirements
chunks.text: formats an SD card so PocketMage can mount it. The device reads a single FAT32 primary partition on an MBR partition table with 32 KB clusters; anything else is not detected reliably. - **Card size:** 2 GB to 32 GB microSD recommended. The slot accepts up to 2 TB, but cards above 32 GB must be forced to FAT32 and MBR and are not recommended. - **Filesystem:** FAT32 - **Partition scheme:** MBR (Master Boot Record) - **Partitions:** a single primary partition - **Cluster (allocation unit) size:** 32 KB - **Sector size:** 512 bytes (default) Not supported: exFAT, GPT partition tables, and 64 GB or larger cards unless you explicitly force FAT32 and MBR.

chunks.text: - **Cluster (allocation unit) size:** 32 KB - **Sector size:** 512 bytes (default) Not supported: exFAT, GPT partition tables, and 64 GB or larger cards unless you explicitly force FAT32 and MBR.

chunks.text: - **Cluster (allocation unit) size:** 32 KB - **Sector size:** 512 bytes (default) Not supported: exFAT, GPT partition tables, and 64 GB or larger cards unless you explicitly force FAT32 and MBR. Insert the card, open **Command Prompt as Administrator**, and run: ```bat diskpart ```

chunks.text: Not supported: exFAT, GPT partition tables, and 64 GB or larger cards unless you explicitly force FAT32 and MBR. chunks.heading: Step 3: Format the card (MBR + FAT32)
chunks.text: disk number that matches your card size. ::: callout warning "Select the correct disk" The next step wipes the disk you select. Confirm the number against the card size before continuing. ::: Replace `X` with your disk number, then run each line in the `diskpart` prompt: ```text select disk X clean convert mbr create partition primary format fs=fat32 unit=32k quick assign exit ```

chunks.heading: Step 4: Verify (optional)
chunks.text: ::: Replace `X` with your disk number, then run each line in the `diskpart` prompt: ```text select disk X clean convert mbr create partition primary format fs=fat32 unit=32k quick assign exit ``` Open **Disk Management**, right-click the disk, and open Properties then Volumes. The partition style must read **Master Boot Record (MBR)**.
